name: Compression framework (LZ4)
verdict_reason: Apple gives no LZ4 numbers, but an independent lzbench run of upstream LZ4 shows 6.2x faster compression and 12.9x faster decompression than zlib's fastest level, in exchange for noticeably larger output.
tier_reason: Independent, reproducible lzbench run, but of the upstream LZ4 library rather than Apple's own implementation in the Compression framework.
claimed_speedup: 550 MB/s vs 89.0 MB/s compression (6.2x) and 3832 MB/s vs 297 MB/s decompression (12.9x) against zlib 1.3.2 -1; output 47.60% of input vs 36.45% (derived from page data)
workload: Silesia corpus (silesia.tar, 212 MB), single thread, whole-file compress and decompress
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, single thread
install: built into iOS 9+ / macOS 10.11+ (Compression framework; NSData.compressed(using: .lz4) on iOS 13+ / macOS 10.15+)
one_liner: Apple's LZ4 codec; upstream LZ4 decompresses 12.9x and compresses 6.2x faster than zlib's fastest level, with larger output.
how_it_is_fast: LZ4 does LZ77 matching with a single hash probe and writes literals and matches as byte-aligned tokens with no entropy coding. Decoding is little more than memcpy of literals and back-references.
use_it_when: Speed matters more than size: caches, IPC, scratch files, in-memory snapshots
Decoding happens often on battery-powered devices
skip_it_when: Bandwidth or storage is the constraint; output is about 30% larger than zlib's here
Interop with third-party LZ4 readers: use COMPRESSION_LZ4_RAW, because COMPRESSION_LZ4 adds Apple's own block framing
caveats: Measures upstream lz4 1.10.0 on x86 Linux, not Apple's implementation on Apple silicon
Apple's documentation gives no LZ4 numbers
tradeoffs: Lowest ratio of the Compression framework algorithms
COMPRESSION_LZ4's framing is not readable by stock LZ4 tools

evidence.quote: The tests were run on a single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P processor at 3.20 GHz
The LZ4 compression algorithm for fast compression.
